the use of hierarchical distance sampling (HDS) models, which accounts for imperfect detection, can provide more realistic estimates of population trends than the commonly used TRIM method.

1) population trend estimates of 13 bird species differed between the TRIM approach, which ignores detection, and the HDS model, which accounts for it; and 2) detection varied among species, observers and years, and this variation was not accounted for when using the TRIM method.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of distance sampling models is recommended for monitoring bird populations, and that this method is especially useful for bird species with a low detectability.

, in order to obtain accurate trend estimates for bird populations, it is necessary to account for imperfect detectability, and this is especially relevant in open habitats where detectability is likely to change from year to year.
, in an open landscape where detectability is not constant, it is important to consider imperfect detection when estimating bird population trends, and that the HDS approach can help in this task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TRIM approach is not suitable for estimating population trends in open Mediterranean farmland landscapes, where detectability is likely to change over time and vary among species.
, to ensure reliable trend estimation, monitoring protocols should include the estimation of detection probability and its variation over time.
the TRIM approach should be complemented with HDS models to obtain reliable population trends.
